column2: Conway's Game of Life on an amber 1-bit screen. PAIR: amber #ffb000 ink on black #000000 ground, like an amber OLED or a plasma terminal. The glass is a Life universe of 2x2-pixel cells (80x40 cells; choose another cell size if it reads better), and the time is made of Life itself: the numerals are built from the game's own stable objects (blocks, beehives, loaves, boats, ships, long snakes and barges laid as strokes) so each digit is a still life a Life player would recognise, counters open, unmistakable at --scale 4. Around them the universe is busy with real patterns: gliders and lightweight spaceships crossing, blinkers, toads, beacons and a pulsar or two oscillating, a glider gun at an edge firing a stream that eaters next to the digits swallow (gliders must never hit the time by accident). Use real B3/S23 rules for the life around the time wherever you can, and keep frame() pure: periodic patterns are closed form (a glider is the same shape every 4 generations, one cell further on); anything chaotic is simulated from a fixed start within the warmup budget. Choose a generation rate so motion reads smooth (e.g. 15-30 generations a second, one cell per step). Minute turn, the centrepiece: a glider (or a salvo) is aimed at the changing digit; on impact the still life ignites into a short chaotic burn that spreads away from the digit and dies out to ash and blinkers (the old digit gone by :00, its open sides never closing into another digit), then after :00 a glider synthesis builds the new digit: a fleet of gliders converges and each collision leaves a block or a beehive in place, the stroke assembling evenly, not stroke by stroke. Hour: a bigger show: e.g. a Gosper gun or a breeder sweeps a front across the universe, or the whole field explodes in a 'methuselah' (R-pentomino, acorn) bloom, while the hour digits stay readable. A tiny HUD in a 1-bit cell-font of your own (generation counter, population) is optional and clearly secondary.

Op art and moiré, the 1960s art of Bridget Riley and Vasarely, plus the scanimation (barrier-grid) trick of old animated books. PAIR: near-white #f0f4ff ink on deep blue #1030c8 ground, like a white-on-blue STN 12864 module. The glass is all lines: fine parallel stripes, concentric rings, checks and waves at 1-2 px pitch, and the numerals are hidden in them the moiré way: inside a numeral the stripes are shifted half a period (or have another angle or pitch), so the digit appears out of the pattern as a crisp, vibrating shape with no outline drawn, and as the stripes drift the digit stays put while everything shimmers. Design ten numerals for this medium (geometric, op-art, bold enough that phase-shift edges read them at --scale 4; the digits may also be denser or a different pattern so they are always the strongest read). Constant dynamic life: the grating drifts and breathes, a second transparent grating slides over the first so moiré fringes sweep across the glass in slow waves, Riley's waves ripple, a Vasarely checkerboard swells into a bulge (flat pattern only: the distortion is a line displacement, not shading). Minute turn, the centrepiece: the changing digit's phase shift dissolves evenly back into the field (gone before :00), then after :00 the new digit's shift grows in from its outline, a moiré interference fringe rolling across it as it locks into phase. Hour: a bigger show: the whole field goes through a sequence of op-art pieces (a Riley wave, a Vasarely sphere-free bulge, a spiral, a scanimation burst where a sliding barrier grid animates a running figure) while the hour digits stay readable. Mind the panel: 1-px high-contrast lines moving fast smear and tear on this glass; keep the motion at ~1 px a frame or slower and render --tear.

Banknote engraving: guilloche rosettes, intaglio line engraving and microprint, the security printing of old currency. PAIR: banknote green ink #1d5a3c on cream paper #efe6c8. The glass is a note: a frame of guilloche borders (dense interlaced lathe curves), one or two big rosettes (spirograph-like rose engine patterns), lines of microtext, a small engraved vignette (an invented allegory: a lighthouse, a steam locomotive or a sheaf of wheat in line engraving, no real person, no real currency, no real country). The numerals are engraved the way banknote denominations are: big ornate numerals filled with fine parallel hatching that swells and bends with the form, outlined by an engraved keyline and a white line inside it, so they read first as engraving and then, unmistakably, as the time; design all ten as a set (the 1-bit line work is the shading: line width and density, never grey). Constant dynamic life: the rose engine is alive: the rosettes' parameters drift so the interlaced curves weave and breathe, a moiré shimmer runs through the guilloche border, microtext scrolls along a band, a security thread glints as a travelling band of inverted lines, the vignette's smoke or waves move in line engraving. Minute turn, the centrepiece: the old numeral's hatching is burnished away evenly (all lines thinning and shortening together, the keyline last, gone before :00), and after :00 an engraver's burin cuts the new numeral: the full keyline first, then the hatch lines ploughed in parallel across it. Hour: a bigger show: e.g. the geometric lathe draws a brand-new rosette live, its pen sweeping loop after loop, while the hour numerals stay readable; or the note turns over (a flat flip by wipe, no 3D) to its reverse with another design. No serial numbers or other numbers that compete with the time.

A formicarium, the ant farm: a thin slice of sand between two panes of glass, seen side-on. PAIR: dark umber ink #2a1a0c on pale sand #e2c48c ground. The sand is a 1-bit stipple texture (ink grains on ground, denser deeper down, a few pebbles and roots), the tunnels are clean ground colour, and the ants are bold solid ink sprites (big enough to read at --scale 4: head, thorax, gaster, six legs that actually walk, antennae; draw them at least ~9x5 px). The time is the colony's own architecture: the numerals are the tunnel system the ants have dug, chambers and galleries shaped into digits (design all ten as tunnel networks: smooth-walled galleries with rounded chamber ends and side chambers, counters solid sand, unmistakable), with a surface strip at the top (grass blades, a crumb, a dropped sugar cube) and a few entrance holes. Constant life: dozens of ants walking the tunnels in both directions at 1 px a frame or slower, stopping, touching antennae, carrying grains, larvae and crumbs, the queen in a chamber, grains trickling, an ant on the surface dragging a crumb home. Minute turn, the centrepiece: the changing digit's galleries are backfilled evenly (ants pack grains along the whole gallery at once, so the tunnel narrows everywhere together, never leaving a partial that reads as another digit; gone before :00), and after :00 they dig the new digit: a thin pilot tunnel along its whole outline first, then it widens to full galleries, grains carried up and dumped on the surface spoil heap. Hour: a bigger show: e.g. a nuptial flight: winged ants pour out of the entrance and flutter up and away across the sky strip, or rain floods down a shaft and the colony rescues its brood, while the time stays readable. Night: the farm under a lamp, ants slower.
